title: The First Years
note: Management Executive and Senior Management Executive (ranks 0-1), which every graduate and poly career passes through, and where a poly entrant can still be in their fifties: nothing here assumes a new or young officer. The run's peer, senior and junior carry the stories. and_team names the peer by what an earlier card remembers (the_work's slides, the post-it workshop's "agree"). Three callbacks pay off years later: copied_in_file and copied_in_repaid follow the peer you did or did not warn, and for_the_record_audit finds the notes you kept.

events.title: One Word

topic.text: why the renewal form asks for the same date three times
whether to extend a pilot by a year

word.a: Your second version is better, and goes up on Thursday. It comes back with the same word. "Discuss", you eventually learn, was never about the paper. It meant come upstairs.
word.b: {senior} reads the paper while you wait, agrees with all four pages, and tells you to send it on as it is. That was the discussion. It took six minutes.
word.c: Your reply says: "Happy to discuss." It comes back: "Discuss." The paper goes up and down the building three more times before anyone books a room.

word.a: The new version opens with the answer to "Why?" in one paragraph. {senior} reads that paragraph, approves the paper, and returns the other three pages unread.
word.b: {senior} explains that "Why?" meant why now, not why at all, and that the answer is a budget cycle you have not yet heard of. You write it down.
word.c: Your reply is one line long, and answers the question. {senior} writes "OK" beneath it. You keep the page in a drawer for years, for no reason you could explain.

word.a: Four pages become two. The new version is also noted. You learn that "Noted" means read, agreed with, and not to be acted on in this financial year.
word.b: {senior} is surprised to see you, and explains kindly that "Noted" is a complete reply. It means the paper was read. It does not mean anything will happen, and nothing does.
word.c: Your reply asks what happens next. It is also noted. Eighteen months later the paper is found in a file, sent up again by someone else, and approved.

word.a: You rewrite it before going up, to be safe. {senior} only wanted to say it was good. There are now two good versions, and a meeting about which one to use.
word.b: You go up at once. {senior} wanted to say it was good, and to put a face to the paper. The meeting takes four minutes. You replay it for a week.
word.c: Your reply says you are free all afternoon. {senior} is not. The meeting happens three weeks later, by which time the paper has gone up anyway, unchanged.

word.a: Four pages become one. {senior} approves it and sends it upstairs, where the next reader writes "Pls elaborate" across the top.
word.b: {senior} explains that the paper is fine, but the person above reads everything on a phone, in a car, between meetings. You learn to write for the car.
word.c: Your one-line reply reads, in full: "Noted." It is the shortest thing you have ever sent upstairs, and {senior} approves the paper on the strength of it.

events.body: Your minute paper on {topic} took a week and runs to four pages. It comes back from {senior}'s office the next morning with one word in the margin: "{word}"

choices.text: Rewrite it from the top.
choices.outcome: {word.a}

choices.text: Go up and ask what the word means.
choices.outcome: {word.b}

choices.text: Send it back up unchanged, with a one-line reply.
choices.outcome: {word.c}

events.title: Friday, 5pm

owner.a: On Monday the CEO's PA writes to ask, politely, about a yoghurt. Your reply quotes paragraph 3. The circular is reissued the following week, with a new paragraph 4, on exemptions.
owner.b: The yoghurt survives six more Fridays. Nothing else in the fridge does, and the floor draws its own conclusions about paragraph 3, mostly at the pantry sink, mostly while you are there.
owner.c: The CEO replies to all forty of you: "Mine. Pls bin. Thanks for checking." It becomes the most forwarded email on the floor that year, and the friendliest.

owner.text: with {peer}'s name and a smiley face
owner.a: {peer} finds the empty shelf on Monday, laughs, and pins a copy of the circular to the fridge door with paragraph 3 highlighted and your initials in the margin.
owner.b: You bin everyone's food but {peer}'s. Nobody says anything. On Monday morning somebody has labelled the milk, the butter and the chilli sauce with {peer}'s name too.
owner.c: Forty people now know that {peer} keeps a yoghurt for eleven days. {peer} collects it from your desk in person, to applause, and bins it.

owner.text: "DO NOT THROW", in capitals, and nothing else
owner.a: You bin it. On Monday a second yoghurt appears, labelled "DO NOT THROW. I MEAN IT." Paragraph 3 holds, and so, it turns out, does whoever it is.
owner.b: The yoghurt stays. By March it has outlasted two committee members and a fridge thermostat, and the floor refers to it, without irony, as the tenant.
owner.c: Nobody claims it. Three people reply to say it is not theirs, and one to ask what paragraph 3 says. At 5pm it goes into the bin anyway.

events.body: The pantry fridge is cleared at 5pm every Friday, under paragraph 3 of a circular, and this quarter the clearing falls to you. Behind the milk sits a yoghurt, eleven days past its date, labelled {owner}.

choices.text: Bin it, as paragraph 3 says.
choices.outcome: {owner.a}

choices.text: Clear everything else, and leave the yoghurt.
choices.outcome: {owner.b}

choices.text: Email the floor, asking the owner to claim it.
choices.outcome: {owner.c}

events.title: And Team

options.text: {peer}, whose half of the slides you once presented as your own,
{peer}, who once put "agree" beside your post-it,

events.body: The {doc} you {doc.made} with {with} goes up to the CEO under your supervisor's name alone. The CEO's reply thanks her "and team". {peer} forwards it to you without a word.

choices.text: Ask her to put both your names on the next one.
choices.outcome: She agrees at once, and seems surprised you had to ask. The next {doc} carries three names, and the CEO's reply thanks "the team". You decide to count it.

choices.text: Reply to the CEO, and name who did the work.
choices.outcome: Your reply runs to two lines and names {peer} first. The CEO answers "Well done both." Your supervisor copies you on nothing for a quarter, then on everything.

choices.text: Say nothing. Papers go up under the name above yours.
choices.outcome: You build the next {doc} too, and it also goes up under her name. In March she is promoted, and asks for you to come with her. {peer} is not asked.

events.title: Copied In

above.text: a Deputy Secretary's and two directors'
the CEO's and the HR director's
a Permanent Secretary's, and nobody else's

events.body: An email arrives with your name in the cc line, beneath {above}. It is marked Official (Closed). It concerns next year's restructuring, and paragraph two abolishes the post of {peer}, from your intake.

choices.text: Tell {peer}, quietly, after work.
choices.outcome: Over kopi, in a sentence that mentions no email, you tell {peer} to look around. {peer} applies for two other posts that week, gets one, and never asks how you knew.

choices.text: Say nothing. It was not sent to you to share.
choices.outcome: The restructuring is announced six weeks later, at a townhall. {peer} hears it with everyone else and is redeployed in good order. You say all the right things, slightly too fluently.

choices.text: Tell the sender you have been copied in error.
choices.outcome: {above.office} thanks you in one line and takes you off the list. Nobody ever says who added you. For a while you open every email expecting to be on it.

events.title: The Cc Line
events.body: {peer}, looking for something else in an old file, has found the email about the restructuring that abolished {peer.their} post. Your name is in its cc line, dated six weeks before anyone told {peer.them}.

choices.text: Explain, properly, over kopi.
choices.outcome: You explain the cc line, and Official (Closed), and the six weeks. {peer} hears you out and says {peer.they} would have done the same. Neither of you is sure that is true.

choices.text: Point out that it was marked Official (Closed).
choices.outcome: {peer} agrees that it was. The conversation is short and entirely correct. After it, {peer} is perfectly cordial to you in every meeting for years, and never once in the lift.

events.title: Face Down
events.body: {peer} comes by, closes the door, and puts a printout on your desk, face down. "You told me once," {peer} says. The header shows through the paper, backwards: next year's postings.

choices.text: Turn it over.
choices.outcome: You are going somewhere difficult, in April. You have three months to make it look like your idea, and you manage it. Nobody upstairs ever learns that you knew first.

choices.text: Leave it face down, and thank {peer}.
choices.outcome: {peer} takes the printout back without a word, and looks almost relieved. In April the postings come out. Yours is somewhere difficult, and you are the only person on the floor who is surprised.

events.title: For the Record

line.text: that the target will not be met this year or next
that the system will miss launch day, and launch day will not move
that the vendor has done this to two other agencies

events.body: You are taking notes at a meeting between {speaker} and three agencies. Forty minutes in, {speaker} says, calmly, {line}. The notes are yours, and are cleared before they go out.

choices.text: Write it down exactly as it was said.
choices.outcome: The notes go out with the line in paragraph six, word for word. Nobody replies to them. A fortnight later you are taken off the meeting's distribution list, and then off the meeting.

choices.text: Write down what was meant, not what was said.
choices.outcome: "The meeting noted the challenges ahead." Cleared in one round, unchanged: the first sentence of yours to go upstairs exactly as you wrote it.

choices.text: Write it down, and flag it when the draft goes up.
choices.outcome: The draft comes back with the line struck through and initialled. The struck draft is filed beside the cleared notes, as drafts are, where anyone who looks can read both.

events.title: The Note-Taker

options.text: your notes of the meeting, line and all
your draft of the notes, with the line struck through

events.body: The Auditor-General's Office is auditing a scheme that went wrong exactly as someone predicted at a meeting. The only record of the prediction is {record}. The auditors would like a word with the note-taker.

choices.text: Confirm the record, and that you wrote it.
choices.outcome: The audit report quotes it in a footnote, unattributed. Everyone who was at that meeting knows who took the notes, and two of them tell you so, in very different tones.

choices.text: Confirm that it is accurate, and nothing more.
choices.outcome: You confirm that it is an accurate record, and add nothing. The footnote appears anyway. What the people in the footnote remember is that you added nothing.

events.title: The Lucky Draw

prize.text: an air fryer, for the third year running

events.body: You are on the D&D committee, having missed the meeting at which the committee was chosen. The theme is {theme}. The top prize is {prize}, and the box holds every name in the division, directors included.

choices.text: Draw it straight, whoever comes out.
choices.outcome: The CEO wins it, and gives it back, to applause. So does a director, and then another. By the fourth draw the prize has been on stage longer than the band.

choices.text: Take the directors' names out before the top prize.
choices.outcome: An officer in her first month wins it and cries a little. The directors, spared the business of giving it back, are quietly grateful. Nobody ever checks the box.

choices.text: Spend the prize money on the food instead.
choices.outcome: The food is the best anyone can remember, and there is no lucky draw. Attendance the next year falls by a third. Nobody, it turns out, came for the food.

events.title: The Internet Laptop
events.body: A vendor has sent {file} as a download link. Your work laptop is not on the internet, by design, and the division's internet laptop is booked until three. {senior} wants it at two.

choices.text: Open it on your phone and email it to your work account.
choices.outcome: {senior} has it at 1:52pm. The next quarter's IT security review reaches you: a forty-minute refresher on IM8, with a quiz at the end and a certificate.

choices.text: Ask the vendor to send it the long way.
choices.outcome: The vendor sends it as one attachment, which is too large, then as six, the fourth of which is quarantined. {senior} has it on Thursday, and asks what happened to Tuesday.

choices.text: Read it on your phone, and retype it.
choices.outcome: Six pages, retyped by 1:58pm, with two typos, both in the vendor's name. Every keystroke was compliant. When you explain how you did it, nobody believes you.

events.title: Station 4

exhibit.text: a poster of the new scheme
a tablet running the new app
a service counter, repainted for the visit

events.body: The Minister is visiting. The run-sheet puts you at Station 4, beside {exhibit}, from 10:42 to 10:45am, with {senior} two steps behind the Minister. At 10:43 the Minister turns and asks you whether it works.

choices.text: Say "not yet, Minister", and why.
choices.outcome: The Minister asks a second question, which is not on the run-sheet, and then a third. The visit leaves Station 4 at 10:49. {senior} never mentions it. It is noted.

choices.text: Give the line from the brief.
choices.outcome: "It is progressing well, Minister." The visit moves on to Station 5 at 10:45 exactly. That evening {senior} sends you a thumbs-up. You do not delete it.

choices.text: Say what would make it work, in ninety seconds.
choices.outcome: The Minister's private secretary writes it down. Station 5 is dropped to make up the time, and the officer at Station 5, who rehearsed for a week, finds you at lunch to say so.

events.title: Standard Operating Procedure
events.body: {junior} has joined your section and been given the standard operating procedures: forty-one pages, last revised two reorganisations ago. You keep your own version on one page of a notebook. Yours is the one that works.

choices.text: Give {junior} your page.
choices.outcome: Your page says which director reads only the first paragraph, which printer jams, and who in HR picks up before nine. {junior} is useful within a week, and photocopies it.

choices.text: Let {junior} learn it the way you did.
choices.outcome: {junior} learns it by getting it wrong in front of the right people. It takes a year. Neither of you mentions it, and {junior} starts a notebook.

choices.text: Rewrite the forty-one pages around your one.
choices.outcome: Three months of evenings. The new procedures are adopted across the division, with your name in the version history and nowhere else, and {junior} reads them in a weekend.

events.title: Approved Leave

away.text: a hotel lobby in Seattle, at 1:40am local time
a hotel room in New York, at 4:40am local time
a beach bar in Honolulu, at 10:40pm the evening before

events.body: Your leave was approved in January. In September the Workplan Seminar is moved onto its second week, by the person who approved it, and your section's slide has nobody else to present it.

choices.text: Cancel the leave and present the slide.
choices.outcome: Your slide is on at 4:40pm, to eleven people and a Deputy Secretary who leaves at 4:42. The airline turns your fare into a voucher, valid for a year. You never use that either.

choices.text: Go. Someone else can present it.
choices.outcome: Your slide is presented, competently, by your reporting officer, who credits you by name. You come back rested, and do the best work of your year in the month that follows.

choices.text: Present it by video, from the holiday.
choices.outcome: From {away}, you present the slide. The connection holds. Afterwards three directors tell you how good it was to see you. Nobody mentions the slide.
